title: Final exam
sub: 19 new problems from every unit: spot the technique, size it from the constraints, pick the collection, predict three traces, catch two traps and explain A* out loud
cards/0/q: Five new problems. Match each one to its technique.
cards/0/pairs/0/0: Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards (#1423): take k cards, each from the left or right end of the row
cards/0/pairs/0/1: A window of length n − k with the smallest sum
cards/0/pairs/1/0: Asteroid Collision (#735): asteroids fly right (+) or left (−), the smaller one explodes on contact; who survives
cards/0/pairs/1/1: A stack of survivors: a left-mover fights the top
cards/0/pairs/2/0: Perfect Squares (#279): fewest perfect squares that sum to n
cards/0/pairs/2/1: Coin change where the coins are 1, 4, 9, …
cards/0/pairs/3/0: Find All Possible Recipes (#2115): dishes made of ingredients that can be dishes themselves
cards/0/pairs/3/1: Kahn: the queue holds what can already be cooked
cards/0/pairs/4/0: Copy List with Random Pointer (#138): deep copy of a list whose random points to any node
cards/0/pairs/4/1: A dictionary from old node to its copy
cards/1/q: Five new problems and a candidate's plan for each. The limit is 1 second, the rule of thumb is about 10⁸ simple operations. Which plans are correct and fit? Select all that apply.
cards/1/options/0: Minimum Knight Moves (#1197): a knight on an infinite board, target with |x|, |y| ≤ 300. BFS from (0, 0) over the cells of a square about 600 wide (a couple of cells of slack past the edge) — ≈ 3.6·10⁵ cells with 8 moves each
cards/1/options/1: Minimum Time to Complete Trips (#2187): up to 10⁵ buses, time[i] and totalTrips up to 10⁷. Try t = 1, 2, 3, … and count the trips in O(n) for each t until there are enough
cards/1/options/2: Find the Difference (#389): t is s shuffled plus one extra letter. XOR of every character of both strings leaves the extra letter: O(n) time, O(1) memory
cards/1/options/3: Edit Distance (#72), but with strings up to 10⁵ characters: keep two rows of the table — O(n) memory, problem solved
cards/1/options/4: Max Number of K-Sum Pairs (#1679): n ≤ 10⁵, each move removes two numbers that sum to k. A dictionary from number to how many are waiting for a partner; for x, look up k − x — O(n)
cards/1/explain: Knight: the states are the cells of the square, ≈ 3.6·10⁵, with 8 times as many moves, ≈ 3·10⁶ — BFS fits. #2187: the answer can reach 10⁷ · 10⁷ = 10¹⁴, so trying every t is hopeless. The number of trips by time t never drops as t grows — a monotone predicate, so binary search on the answer: ≈ 47 checks of O(n) each, with trips counted in long. XOR cancels every letter that has a pair and leaves the extra one. Two table rows save memory, not time: n·m = 10¹⁰ cells. #1679 is Two Sum with a counter: partner found — decrement the count of k − x; not found — increment the count of x.
cards/2/task: Map of Highest Peak (#1765): water has height 0, neighbouring cells differ by at most 1, and the highest peak must be as high as possible. A land cell's height is its distance to the nearest water, and one BFS from all the water at once computes them. On the rig the water cells are the zeros, (1, 1) and (3, 5). The rig will stop twice and ask what the code does next.
cards/2/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: (0, 1), the first neighbour of (1, 1): one water source's wave runs to the end first
cards/2/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: (3, 5), the second water cell: it is in the queue ahead of the neighbours of (1, 1)
cards/2/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Nothing: every cell next to water already has height 1
cards/2/goal/asks/0/q: Water cell (1, 1) is done: its four neighbours got height 1 and joined the queue. Which cell does the code take next?
cards/2/goal/asks/0/explain: Both water cells entered the queue at the very start with height 0, and the queue hands cells out in order: everything at distance 0 leaves before anything at distance 1. The waves grow together, layer by layer, so the nearest water reaches each cell first. If the search ran from (1, 1) alone first, cell (2, 5) would get 5 instead of 1.
cards/2/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: It gets 4 now and 4 again from (1, 4): two entries in the queue
cards/2/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: It gets 8 — 4 from each water cell
cards/2/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: It gets 4 and enters the queue once: by the time (1, 4) is taken, the height is already set
cards/2/goal/asks/1/q: Layer 3: we take (0, 3). Its neighbour (0, 4) is still «?», and it is 4 steps from both water cells. What happens to (0, 4)?
cards/2/goal/asks/1/explain: The height is set when a cell is added to the queue, and the «already set?» check keeps it from entering twice — the very next event, (1, 4), shows that. A tie between the two water cells changes nothing: both give 4. For #1765 that is the answer too: the cell cannot be higher than 4, because along the shortest path to water the height drops by at most 1 per step. Result: highest peak 4, in O(R·C).
cards/3/q: Furthest Building You Can Reach (#1642): up to 10⁵ buildings, walking left to right. Going down is free; climbing d costs d bricks or one ladder. Up to 10⁹ bricks, up to n ladders. How far can we get? What do you use?
cards/3/options/0: A min-heap of climbs sized ladders: ladders go to the largest climbs seen so far; when it overflows, the smallest one is paid in bricks
cards/3/options/1: Greedy as you go: ladders on the first climbs, bricks once the ladders run out
cards/3/options/2: DP over the state (building, bricks left, ladders left)
cards/3/explain: A ladder pays off most on the largest climb, and which climbs are largest is only known for the ones already passed. This is «top k» on a min-heap: it holds the climbs under ladders, and the root is the smallest of them. Once the heap grows past ladders, Dequeue — that climb is paid in bricks; bricks below zero means we cannot go on. O(n log L) time and O(L) memory, where L is the number of ladders.
cards/3/wrong/1: Heights [1, 2, 12], 9 bricks, one ladder. The ladder goes on the climb of 1, and 9 bricks are not enough for the climb of 10 — stuck at building 1. The optimum: a brick for 1, the ladder for 10 — we reach the end.
cards/3/wrong/2: Up to 10⁹ bricks: 10⁵ · 10⁹ states fit neither in time nor in memory.
cards/4/q: Search a 2D Matrix (#74): rows are sorted, and each row starts above the end of the previous one — read row by row, it is one sorted array. Tests on square matrices pass, but on [[1,3,5,7],[10,11,16,20],[23,30,34,60]] with target = 60 the code throws IndexOutOfRangeException. Tap the buggy line.
cards/4/explain: A flat index splits by the row width: row mid / cols, column mid % cols — just like cell y · w + x of a flat grid. The code divides by rows. In a square matrix rows = cols, so the bug stays hidden. Here rows = 3 and cols = 4: mid = 10 gives row 10 / 3 = 3, and there are only three rows. The fix is matrix[mid / cols][mid % cols]; the search is O(log(m·n)).
cards/5/q: A Unity project (.NET Standard 2.1). Time Based Key-Value Store (#981): Set(key, value, timestamp) and Get(key, timestamp) — the value with the largest time ≤ timestamp, or an empty string. Times in Set calls strictly increase, timestamp is up to 10⁷, up to 2·10⁵ calls. What do you store?
cards/5/options/0: A dictionary from key to a list of (time, value) pairs: Set appends — the list is already sorted; Get binary-searches the last time ≤ timestamp
cards/5/options/1: Dictionary<(string, int), string>: Get tries timestamp, timestamp − 1, … until a record is found
cards/5/options/2: Dictionary<string, SortedSet<int>> for the times plus a dictionary of values; Get is GetViewBetween(0, timestamp).Max
cards/5/options/3: One List of (key, time, value) records: Get walks back from the end to the first record with that key and time ≤ timestamp
cards/5/explain: Times arrive in increasing order, so there is nothing to sort: Add at the end is amortized O(1), and the list stays sorted. Get looks for the last time ≤ timestamp: upper_bound − 1, or ~i − 1 from BinarySearch, like the level from the XP thresholds. O(log n) per Get, O(n) memory.
cards/5/wrong/1: Up to 10⁷ empty timestamps can lie between two records: one Get costs up to 10⁷ dictionary lookups.
cards/5/wrong/2: On .NET Core 3.0+ this is O(log n), but in Unity the GetViewBetween view recounts the elements of the range — O(k), here up to every record of the key. And no tree is needed: the times already arrive in order.
cards/5/wrong/3: Get is O(n): 2·10⁵ calls over 2·10⁵ records — up to 4·10¹⁰ comparisons.
cards/6/task: My Calendar III (#732): bookings are [start, end), and after each Book you return the largest k — how many bookings overlap at one moment; up to 400 calls. The last Book returns the peak over all bookings, and a sweep computes it: on the rig the bookings are meetings and the peak is the number of rooms. The rig will stop twice and ask what the code does next.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Takes the free room R1, the peak stays 2
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: New peak 3: no free room, opens R3
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: t = 5: [5, 9) starts. Right now [2, 6) is in R2 and [4, 7) is in R1. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: R1 was freed at 4 and went straight to [4, 7) — both rooms are busy. A third booking at the same time is a new peak of 3: at moment 5, [2, 6), [4, 7) and [5, 9) overlap.
cards/6/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: The end of [2, 6): 2 remain, R2 is freed
cards/6/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: The start of [6, 8): 4 at once, new peak 4
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: t = 6: [2, 6) ends and [6, 8) starts. Three bookings are running. Which does the code handle first?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: Bookings are half-open: at moment 6, [2, 6) is already over and does not overlap [6, 8). So at equal times an end goes before a start — when sorting events, −1 before +1. Start first would give a false peak of 4. The answer for #732 is 3; with 400 calls, a fresh sweep on every Book is O(n² log n), around 3·10⁶ operations.
cards/7/q: Path Sum III (#437): a tree of up to 1000 nodes, values up to ±10⁹. How many downward paths — from a node to one of its descendants, not necessarily from the root or to a leaf — sum to targetSum? The interviewer asks for O(n). What do you do?
cards/7/options/0: Prefix sums of the root path in a dictionary from sum to count: at a node add count[sum − target], go into the children, and remove your own sum on the way back
cards/7/options/1: A sliding window over the path from the root: extend downwards, shrink from the top while the sum exceeds target
cards/7/options/2: Start a downward traversal from every node and add up the sums
cards/7/explain: A downward path is a segment of the path from the root, and a segment's sum is the difference of two prefixes: this is Subarray Sum Equals K on a tree. The dictionary must hold only the prefixes of the current node's ancestors, so on the way back you subtract your own sum — like «choose and undo» in backtracking. The initial count[0] = 1 stands for a path from the root itself. Keep the sum in long: 1000 values of 10⁹ do not fit in int. O(n) time, O(h) memory.
cards/7/wrong/1: A window needs non-negative numbers: with negatives the sum can grow while you shrink, and moving the ends loses answers.
cards/7/wrong/2: That is O(n·h): on a chain of 1000 nodes ≈ 5·10⁵ steps. It passes on LeetCode, but it is not the O(n) you were asked for.
cards/8/q: A leaderboard (Design A Leaderboard, #1244): AddScore(id, score) adds points to a player, Top(k) is the total of the k best scores. What does Top(2) return after AddScore(1, 50), AddScore(2, 50), AddScore(3, 40)?
cards/8/explain: SortedSet treats elements with CompareTo == 0 as the same, and the comparer looks only at the score. Player 2 with the same 50 is a «duplicate» of player 1: Add returned false, and player 2 is not on the board. Top(2) = 50 + 40 = 90. Worse, Remove(p) deletes whoever has the same score — it can wipe someone else's entry. The fix is a unique key: on equal scores compare Id — (a, b) => a.Score != b.Score ? b.Score.CompareTo(a.Score) : a.Id.CompareTo(b.Id).
cards/8/wrong/1: That would be right if all three were in the set. But player 2 is not there: Add silently returned false.
cards/8/wrong/2: Top(2) takes the first two elements, not all of them. Even Top(3) would return 90 here: the set holds only two entries.
cards/8/wrong/3: No exception: Add on a «duplicate» simply returns false, and foreach does not modify the set.
cards/9/task: Increasing Triplet Subsequence (#334): is there i < j < k with nums[i] < nums[j] < nums[k]? You need O(n) time and O(1) memory. This is LIS on tails with tails cut down to two cells, first and second: as soon as x is larger than both, a triplet exists. The rig runs the full tails on [5, 8, 3, 6, 1, 7, 4]. It will stop twice and ask what the code does next.
cards/9/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Nothing: 6 is not larger than the last tail
cards/9/goal/asks/0/q: tails = [3, 8]. Next comes x = 6. What does the code do?
cards/9/goal/asks/0/explain: lower_bound(6) in [3, 8] is index 1: the first tail ≥ 6 is 8. A pair of length 2 now ends at 6 (3, 6) instead of 8, which makes it easier for the next numbers to extend. In the #334 version this is the «x ≤ second → second = x» branch.
cards/9/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: Nothing: 1 comes after 6, so there is no triplet in order
cards/9/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: Appends 7: length 3 — a triplet exists, for example 3, 6, 7
cards/9/goal/asks/1/q: tails = [1, 6], even though 1 comes after 6 in the array. Next comes x = 7. What does the code do, and what does #334 answer?
cards/9/goal/asks/1/explain: Tail 6 means there is a pair of length 2 ending at 6 — namely 3, 6, with 3 earlier. Replacing 3 with 1 did not cancel that pair; it only remembered a smaller start for future pairs. 7 is larger than both tails, so we append: length 3, triplet 3, 6, 7. tails [1, 6, 7] itself is not a subsequence — only the length matches. In #334 this is the «x > second → return true» branch: two variables instead of an array, O(n) and O(1).
cards/10/q: Unity interview: a turn-based tactics game on a 64 × 64 map, 8 directions, a straight step costs 10, a diagonal 14, and swamp costs three times as much. On click you need the cheapest path for a unit. Put the steps of your answer in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: step and swamp costs, one target or many, does the map change, how many units search per turn
cards/10/items/1: Baseline: BFS does not fit — steps cost different amounts; Dijkstra is correct but expands cells in every direction
cards/10/items/2: Idea: A* — a heap by f = g + h, where g is the cost so far including swamp
cards/10/items/3: h is octile, 10·max + 4·min: swamp only costs more, so h never overestimates
cards/10/items/4: Implementation: struct nodes in an array by cell index, your own binary heap, a search number instead of clearing
cards/10/items/5: Dry run: a small map with swamp across the way — the path goes around it if that is cheaper
cards/10/items/6: Cost and edge cases: worst case O(E log V), like Dijkstra; the target is a wall or unreachable
cards/10/explain: Start with the movement model and costs: both the algorithm and h depend on them. Then the baseline and its weakness, the idea and the condition on h — with swamp you have to say why octile stays admissible: every step costs at least what it assumes. The engineering part is what a Unity interviewer waits for: no class Node, no clearing arrays, no PriorityQueue, which Unity does not have. The dry run, the cost and the edge cases come last.
cards/11/q: The cost of this exam's solutions. What is true? Select all that apply.
cards/11/options/0: Map of Highest Peak on 1000 × 1000 is one BFS from all the water: each cell enters the queue once, ≈ 10⁶ steps
cards/11/options/1: Furthest Building: the heap must hold every climb passed so far, or the answer is wrong
cards/11/options/2: Increasing Triplet: two variables replace the tails array — O(n) time and O(1) memory
cards/11/options/3: My Calendar III: handling a start before an end at equal times does not change the answer
cards/11/options/4: Unity has no PriorityQueue: for A* and Furthest Building use your own binary heap on an array, or a SortedSet with a unique key
cards/11/explain: A wave from many sources is O(R·C). The Furthest Building heap holds only the climbs under ladders, at most ladders of them: O(n log L). The triplet needs only the tails of lengths 1 and 2. Start before end counts [2, 6) touching [6, 8) as an overlap — the peak comes out too high. PriorityQueue arrived in .NET 6 and is missing in Unity; SortedSet is there, but it needs a unique key such as (f, cell), or equal entries collapse — as on the leaderboard.
